details.SocialEmotional: At two months, infants begin to engage socially with caregivers and show early emotional development. They smile responsively at familiar people, especially parents or consistent caregivers. Their eyes begin to light up when they see a face, signaling emotional recognition. Infants enjoy being held, rocked, or talked to and can become calm in response to comforting tones. They start to turn toward voices and expressions of warmth. Their crying becomes more purposeful, as they learn that it brings adult attention. They may briefly soothe themselves by sucking on their hands or fingers. Eye contact becomes more consistent during feeding and interaction.
details.Communication: At this age, babies begin to coo and make gurgling sounds during calm, alert states. They turn their heads toward familiar voices and become more attentive when spoken to. Their cries vary in pitch and tone depending on whether they're hungry, tired, or uncomfortable. Infants become quiet or excited when they hear a caregiver's soothing voice. They start to use their voice as a tool for engagement, producing sounds to gain attention. They enjoy face-to-face interactions and may begin to mimic facial expressions or mouth movements.
details.Cognitive: Two-month-old infants are alert and curious during wakeful periods, beginning to notice patterns in their surroundings. They stare at faces for longer durations and follow moving objects with their eyes. They show a preference for high-contrast visuals and human faces. Their brain begins organizing sensory experiences, such as sounds and sights, into memory. They may begin to expect certain routines, like feeding after waking. They start to recognize their caregiver’s scent and voice, demonstrating early memory formation. Their reactions to stimuli become more intentional, like kicking when excited.
details.Physical: Physically, babies at two months show greater head control than at birth but still need neck support. They begin to lift their head briefly during tummy time, strengthening neck and shoulder muscles. Movements of the arms and legs become smoother and more intentional. They can bring their hands to their mouth and may suck on their fists. Muscle tone improves gradually, with the body becoming less curled. Babies may attempt to push against surfaces with their feet when held upright. Their grip reflex persists, allowing them to hold onto a finger or toy briefly. They often move their limbs in response to sound or visual stimulation

details.SocialEmotional: Four-month-olds smile spontaneously and especially enjoy social interaction. They begin to imitate facial expressions such as smiling or frowning. Babies enjoy playing with people and might cry when the play stops. They show clear excitement when caregivers enter the room. They express joy through squeals and laughter. Emotion becomes more visible, especially happiness and frustration. They enjoy games like peek-a-boo and respond with smiles. They become more aware of the tone of voice and facial cues. They start to differentiate familiar people from strangers. Emotional bonds strengthen with daily interaction and physical closeness.
details.Communication: Babies begin to babble, combining vowel and consonant sounds like 'ba' or 'ga'. They use a wider variety of cries to express different needs. They mimic tones, smiling or making noises in response to speech. Babies become excited when they hear music or their caregiver's voice. They follow sounds with improved accuracy, turning their head. They may try to 'talk back' by making sounds during conversation. Eye contact becomes an important part of communication. They enjoy babbling alone or with others. They begin associating sound with events, like hearing a bottle and anticipating feeding. Communication becomes more expressive and intentional.
details.Cognitive: Four-month-olds show greater interest in exploring the environment. They track objects with their eyes and begin to reach for them. They examine hands and fingers, studying their movements. Babies understand simple patterns and begin to anticipate routines. They respond with excitement to familiar toys or games. They show curiosity by staring at new people or items. They begin using their eyes and hands together to explore. They may repeat actions that produce interesting effects, like shaking a rattle. Their attention span is still short but increasing slowly. These skills reflect growing brain organization and awareness.
details.Physical: Babies at this age hold their head steady without support. They push down with their legs when feet are on a hard surface. They can roll from tummy to back with effort. Arm movements become more controlled, allowing them to swat at toys. They bring hands to mouth regularly. They may begin to grab objects and hold them briefly. Tummy time becomes more active, with baby pushing up on elbows. They can sit with support, like in a baby seat. Legs kick strongly during active times. These physical changes reflect developing core strength and coordination.

details.SocialEmotional: Six-month-old babies recognize familiar people and begin to show preferences. They smile at themselves in the mirror and react with joy. They respond to emotions in others, sometimes crying when another baby cries. Babies may show shyness or wariness around strangers. They enjoy social games and show anticipation, laughing before tickles or funny faces. They begin to differentiate caregivers from others. They turn toward voices with enthusiasm. They express joy, frustration, and excitement with more control. Attachment to caregivers strengthens, and they often reach to be held. They prefer familiar settings and may protest when moved suddenly.
details.Communication: Babies respond to their name and turn to locate speakers. They make more complex babbling sounds like 'ba-ba' or 'da-da'. Vocal play increases, with babies experimenting with pitch and volume. They express excitement vocally and through body movement. They take turns in vocal exchanges, waiting after making a sound. Facial expressions accompany many vocalizations. They may stop babbling and listen when someone speaks. They use different cries to signal specific needs. They enjoy music and respond with movement or cooing. Their sounds become more connected to social interaction.
details.Cognitive: Six-month-olds explore objects by mouthing, shaking, and banging them. They pass items from one hand to the other. They watch objects fall and may look to see where they went. They begin to understand object permanence, realizing toys don’t disappear forever. Babies look intently at new faces or items. They search for partially hidden toys. They recognize familiar sounds and may look toward the source. Their attention span increases slightly. They explore cause-and-effect relationships, like banging a toy to make noise. Curiosity drives much of their play and exploration.
details.Physical: Babies can roll over both ways and push up fully on their arms during tummy time. They sit with support and may begin to sit briefly unaided. They bear weight on legs when held upright. They reach for and grasp toys accurately. They begin to bounce in a standing position. Muscle tone improves in the trunk and legs. They transfer objects from hand to hand with ease. Fine motor skills allow for better grip. They may rake small objects toward themselves. Daily tummy time boosts core strength and coordination.

details.SocialEmotional: Nine-month-old babies begin showing strong preferences for caregivers and familiar faces. They may experience stranger anxiety and cling to parents in unfamiliar situations. Social play like peek-a-boo or pat-a-cake brings visible joy. They smile, laugh, and may imitate facial expressions. They observe how caregivers respond to new situations, using social referencing. They start using gestures like reaching out to be picked up. They express a broader range of emotions, including frustration. They enjoy interactive games and anticipate the fun parts. Attachment is evident in how they seek comfort from familiar adults. Their personality becomes more noticeable through daily interactions.
details.Communication: Babies begin to understand simple words like 'no' and may respond to their name consistently. They use more varied babbling, such as 'mamama' and 'dadada'. They mimic sounds and gestures during communication. Babies engage in vocal turn-taking with caregivers. They watch faces closely when someone is talking. They express excitement with squeals and other vocalizations. They respond to tone and volume, quieting or becoming alert as needed. They begin to show understanding through gestures, like pointing or reaching. Early word comprehension develops through daily repetition. They enjoy listening to songs, rhymes, and simple stories.
details.Cognitive: Nine-month-olds develop object permanence and may search for hidden items. They explore objects by banging, dropping, and shaking them. They follow the path of moving objects and show interest in cause-and-effect activities. They imitate simple actions, like clapping or waving. They explore toys with buttons or textures. They begin to recognize familiar objects, even partially covered. Their ability to anticipate events grows, such as expecting a toy when a box is shaken. They look for things they see you hide. They begin sorting toys by how they function. Their curiosity leads to increased problem-solving through trial and error.
details.Physical: Babies can sit independently and transition between positions. They pull themselves up to stand using furniture. They may crawl, scoot, or shuffle to get around. Their grip becomes more refined, using thumb and forefinger to pick up small items (pincer grasp). They explore by reaching, banging, and passing items hand-to-hand. They enjoy bouncing in a standing position. Some may cruise along furniture. They can support some of their weight while standing. They respond with physical excitement to toys or people. Mobility increases rapidly, requiring closer supervision.

details.SocialEmotional: At one year, children often show clear attachment to caregivers and may cry when they leave. They enjoy interactive games and bring toys or books to adults. They show affection through hugs or clinging. They imitate adult behaviors, like talking on a phone or pretending to cook. They express a wide range of emotions, including joy, frustration, and fear. They may begin to show preferences for certain people or toys. They start exploring their environment but check back with caregivers for reassurance. Separation anxiety can be strong at this stage. They recognize themselves in mirrors and may smile or make faces. Daily routines provide a sense of comfort and security.
details.Communication: Children say basic words like 'mama', 'dada', and one or two others. They point to show interest and wave 'bye-bye'. They understand simple instructions like 'come here'. They mimic sounds and tones they hear from others. They babble with speech-like patterns. They recognize names of familiar people, pets, or objects. They begin labeling familiar things when asked. They respond to simple questions with gestures or single words. They show excitement when they hear familiar songs or stories. Communication becomes a two-way process, using both words and actions.
details.Cognitive: One-year-olds explore the world through trial and error. They experiment with how objects work, like placing lids on containers. They search for hidden items and remember where favorite toys are kept. They enjoy simple problem-solving tasks like stacking or dropping blocks. They recognize themselves and familiar people in photos. They mimic daily routines such as brushing hair or pretending to eat. They investigate cause and effect by dropping food or toys. They explore textures and shapes with their hands. They develop preferences for toys and activities. Repetition helps them learn new skills quickly.
details.Physical: Children pull up to stand and may begin taking steps independently. They can cruise along furniture and stoop to pick things up. They sit confidently and move between sitting and crawling. Their fine motor skills allow them to feed themselves with fingers. They enjoy filling and emptying containers. They bang objects together and stack a few blocks. They may hold crayons and make marks on paper. They use both hands to explore and play. They begin removing simple clothing items like hats or socks. Active movement is constant and helps with balance and coordination.

details.SocialEmotional: Fifteen-month-olds show affection to familiar people and may greet them with hugs or cuddles. They seek comfort from caregivers when upset or uncertain. They begin to assert independence, sometimes with frustration. They show pride in achievements like stacking blocks or walking. They imitate everyday tasks such as sweeping or using a spoon. They may throw tantrums when routines change. They enjoy being around other children but may not play cooperatively yet. They may smile or laugh when others do, showing emotional connection. They develop stronger attachment to comfort objects. Emotional awareness is emerging as they learn boundaries and rules.
details.Communication: At this stage, children use around 3–10 clear words regularly. They understand many more words than they can say. They respond to requests like 'give me the ball'. They use gestures along with speech, like pointing while saying a word. They imitate sounds and may try to repeat new words. They enjoy naming familiar people and objects. They respond to simple stories and songs by pointing to pictures or moving. They begin to ask for things with one word or gesture. They listen closely when spoken to and may follow simple directions. Their communication is intentional and tied to getting needs met.
details.Cognitive: Fifteen-month-olds point to body parts when asked and enjoy interactive books. They test cause and effect by pushing buttons or flipping switches. They show interest in puzzles or toys with moving parts. They imitate actions seen in adults, such as talking into a phone. They begin to group similar objects, like cars or animals. They solve simple problems, such as how to reach a high toy. They experiment with dropping objects from different heights. They begin to understand daily routines and may anticipate what’s next. They explore how objects can be used together, like spoon and bowl. Curiosity leads to constant exploration and learning.
details.Physical: Most toddlers at this stage walk independently. They can squat down and return to standing. They may begin to run with stiff, unsure steps. They climb onto low furniture or stairs with assistance. They drink from a cup and may try using a spoon. Their hand coordination allows them to place blocks or sort objects. They enjoy pushing and pulling toys. They begin to undress themselves by removing shoes or hats. They stack two to three blocks and scribble with crayons. Movement becomes more intentional and less reflexive.

details.SocialEmotional: Eighteen-month-olds show increasing independence, often wanting to do things on their own. They may resist help, saying 'no'. They begin to show empathy, such as comforting a crying friend. They enjoy pretend play, imitating adult roles like cooking or driving. They show interest in other children and might begin to play beside them, though not yet engage in cooperative play. They have a growing sense of autonomy, often asserting preferences. They may start to have favorites in food, toys, or people. They become increasingly aware of their emotions and others', though still learning to manage frustration. They respond with affection when comforted.
details.Communication: Eighteen-month-olds begin to use more words and may have a vocabulary of 10 to 20 words. They often repeat words they hear from adults. They understand more than they can say and may follow two-step commands. They use simple phrases like 'want cookie'. They enjoy pointing to body parts and familiar objects when named. They may start using pronouns like 'me' or 'mine'. They often babble along with songs or stories. They point to objects they want and may ask for them by name. Their communication is becoming more interactive and social.
details.Cognitive: At this stage, toddlers enjoy exploring their environment by looking in drawers or under tables. They may start to match colors and shapes and complete simple puzzles. They experiment with different ways to play with toys, like stacking blocks or lining up cars. They show curiosity by opening and closing containers. They understand that items can serve different purposes, like a spoon for eating. They begin to understand basic concepts like 'big' and 'small'. Memory improves, allowing them to recognize familiar places and people quickly.
details.Physical: Eighteen-month-olds walk steadily and may begin running, though still unsteady. They can climb onto low furniture and begin to kick or throw balls. They can feed themselves with utensils and drink from a cup. They are able to stack two or three blocks. They point to objects they want and start to imitate adult actions like brushing teeth. Fine motor skills allow them to scribble with crayons or draw simple lines. They may begin to open doors, drawers, or containers with ease. Their balance and coordination are steadily improving.

details.SocialEmotional: At two years, toddlers become more independent and assertive. They may begin to exhibit signs of defiance, often using the word 'no' as a way to assert control. They are learning to navigate social interactions with others, showing interest in other children but still engaging mostly in parallel play. They begin to demonstrate affection through hugs and kisses. They may start to experience mood swings, with frustration leading to tantrums. However, they also begin to show empathy, comforting others who are upset. Separation anxiety may decrease, but some toddlers may still struggle with transitions.
details.Communication: Two-year-olds have a vocabulary of 50–100 words and may begin to combine two to three words into simple sentences. They understand and follow simple commands like 'give me the ball' or 'come here'. They can name familiar objects, people, and animals. They might use words like 'I', 'you', and 'me' to assert their independence. They begin to engage in simple conversations and can understand basic questions. Pronunciation is still developing, but they can make their needs known. They may enjoy repeating songs or rhymes they hear.
details.Cognitive: At this age, toddlers are exploring their world more intentionally. They begin to understand simple concepts like 'big' and 'small', 'in' and 'out', and 'up' and 'down'. They start solving simple puzzles and can stack blocks or fit shapes into corresponding holes. They have a better understanding of cause and effect, such as pressing a button to make a sound. They may engage in pretend play, such as feeding a doll or pretending to cook. Memory improves, allowing them to remember routines and familiar places.
details.Physical: Two-year-olds can run, jump, and walk up stairs with assistance. They begin to climb with more confidence. Their fine motor skills improve, allowing them to stack blocks, scribble with crayons, and feed themselves with a spoon or fork. They can turn pages in a book and may begin to show interest in dressing themselves, though assistance is often needed. They can kick a ball and throw objects overhand. Physical coordination is improving, though they may still be unsteady on their feet at times.
details.Self-Care: Toddlers may begin to show an interest in toileting, although they may not be fully potty trained. They can drink from a cup without help and may try to brush their teeth with guidance. They can also help with tasks like picking up toys or putting on shoes.

details.SocialEmotional: At 30 months, toddlers begin to engage more in interactive play with other children, such as sharing toys or taking turns. They start to show more empathy, comforting friends or parents when they are upset. They may start to engage in simple cooperative play, like building a tower with blocks together. They begin to understand the concept of rules, even if they don’t always follow them. They are increasingly able to manage frustration and begin to understand the emotional cues of others. They are more independent but still rely on caregivers for emotional support.
details.Communication: By 30 months, toddlers have a vocabulary of 150–300 words and are using 3–4 word sentences. They can understand and follow simple directions with multiple steps, such as 'pick up the toy and put it on the shelf'. They begin to ask questions, such as 'what's that?' or 'why?'. Pronunciation is clearer, though some sounds may still be difficult. They start to engage in more complex conversations, though they still may need support in developing conversational skills. They may enjoy reciting favorite rhymes or stories from memory.
details.Cognitive: Thirty-month-olds begin to understand more abstract concepts, such as size and quantity. They are able to sort objects by color, shape, or size and can complete more complex puzzles. They begin to recognize and identify some letters and numbers. They enjoy activities that require problem-solving, like building with blocks or playing memory games. They are able to engage in more complex pretend play, such as setting up a pretend store or having a tea party. Their memory improves, and they begin to recall past events or experiences.
details.Physical: At 30 months, toddlers can walk confidently and may be able to run, jump, and climb with greater coordination. They are able to pedal a tricycle and kick a ball with some accuracy. Their fine motor skills continue to improve, and they can draw simple shapes like circles and lines. They can begin to put on some clothing with assistance, such as pulling up pants or putting on a shirt. They may begin to use scissors with guidance. Their balance improves, and they become more confident in their physical abilities.
details.Self-Care: At 30 months, toddlers may show increasing interest in self-care tasks. They may start to show signs of readiness for potty training, though many children may still need assistance. They can begin to brush their teeth with help and wash their hands independently. They may also try to feed themselves without help, though they may still make a mess.

details.SocialEmotional: By three years, children become more engaged in social interactions with their peers. They begin to play cooperatively, such as sharing toys, taking turns, and engaging in imaginative play together. They still struggle with impulse control, but they are learning how to express their feelings and emotions in more socially appropriate ways. They begin to assert independence, saying things like 'I can do it myself' and are proud of their achievements. They are more aware of the emotions of others and may comfort a friend or parent when they are upset.
details.Communication: Three-year-olds have a vocabulary of 300–1,000 words and are able to form 4–5 word sentences. They can use language to express thoughts, needs, and desires. They begin to use more complex sentence structures, such as 'I want to play with the red truck'. They can answer simple questions and can recall recent events. They begin to understand the concept of time, using words like 'today', 'tomorrow', or 'yesterday'. Their pronunciation improves, and they are easier to understand.
details.Cognitive: By three years, children are able to solve more complex problems, such as completing simple puzzles with multiple pieces. They understand basic concepts of size, shape, and color and may start to understand numbers and counting. They enjoy engaging in pretend play, taking on roles like a parent, teacher, or superhero. They can also sort objects by color, shape, or category. Their ability to focus and attend to tasks increases, and they are able to complete simple tasks independently.
details.Physical: Three-year-olds run, jump, and climb with greater ease and coordination. They are able to catch and throw a ball with some accuracy. Fine motor skills improve, allowing them to draw recognizable shapes, such as circles, squares, and triangles. They can begin to dress themselves with minimal help, including putting on shoes, socks, and jackets. Their handwriting is still developing, but they may be able to scribble and attempt to write their name.
details.Self-Care: At three years, many children are fully potty trained during the day and may be ready for nighttime training. They can wash and dry their hands independently and brush their teeth with minimal help. They may begin to manage simple personal hygiene tasks, like wiping their nose or combing their hair.

details.SocialEmotional: At four years old, children are becoming more independent and social. They engage in cooperative play, often negotiating roles in pretend play or games with peers. They begin to understand the concept of friendship and may have a 'best friend'. They can manage frustration better and express themselves more clearly. They begin to understand and follow rules in games and may experience disappointment when losing. Empathy continues to develop, and they show concern for others who are upset or hurt.
details.Communication: Four-year-olds have a vocabulary of around 1,000 words and can form sentences with 5–6 words. They are able to express ideas and thoughts in clear, full sentences. They understand and use more complex language, including questions like 'why?' and 'how?' They enjoy telling stories and can recall events from the past. Their speech becomes clearer and easier to understand. They may begin to understand the concept of opposites and can follow multi-step directions.
details.Cognitive: At four years old, children are able to solve problems that require logical thinking. They can understand and perform basic math concepts, such as counting objects and recognizing simple patterns. They enjoy playing games that require rules and memory. They are developing a sense of time and can understand concepts like 'before' and 'after'. They enjoy learning about the world around them and ask a lot of questions. Their attention span increases, and they can focus on tasks for longer periods.
details.Physical: Four-year-olds run, jump, and climb with agility and confidence. They can hop on one foot and catch and throw a ball with better accuracy. Fine motor skills allow them to draw simple figures, such as a person with a head, body, and limbs. They can cut with scissors and are learning to write some letters. They can dress themselves independently and manage basic hygiene tasks, such as brushing teeth and using the toilet.
details.Self-Care: By four years old, children are able to dress themselves with minimal help. They can brush their teeth with supervision and wash their hands without assistance. They are becoming more independent with toileting, though they may need reminders. They can handle simple personal hygiene tasks, such as combing their hair.

details.SocialEmotional: At five years old, children are developing strong social skills. They play cooperatively with peers, taking turns, negotiating rules, and resolving conflicts on their own. They understand the concept of rules and can follow them during games. They have stronger friendships and can understand the emotions of others. They show greater empathy and are able to comfort others in distress. They are becoming more independent but still seek reassurance from caregivers. They may have a clear sense of self and are proud of their accomplishments.
details.Communication: Five-year-olds have a vocabulary of over 2,000 words and can communicate clearly with full sentences. They use language to express their thoughts, ideas, and feelings. They can engage in longer conversations and can tell stories with a beginning, middle, and end. They understand the rules of conversation, such as taking turns and listening to others. Their pronunciation is almost completely clear, and they can express themselves confidently.
details.Cognitive: Five-year-olds are becoming increasingly skilled in problem-solving and critical thinking. They can understand and apply basic math concepts, like addition and subtraction. They enjoy activities that require thinking, such as puzzles and memory games. They are becoming more aware of the world around them and may show interest in science, nature, or other educational topics. They are developing a sense of time and can understand concepts like 'before', 'after', and 'yesterday'. Their ability to focus on tasks and learn new skills continues to grow.
details.Physical: Five-year-olds are becoming more coordinated and agile. They can run, jump, skip, and climb with confidence. They can catch and throw a ball with accuracy. Fine motor skills are well-developed, allowing them to write letters and numbers and draw detailed pictures. They can cut with scissors and may begin to tie their own shoes. They are able to perform basic self-care tasks independently, such as brushing teeth, dressing, and feeding themselves.
details.Self-Care: At five years old, children are able to dress themselves fully and take care of personal hygiene without assistance. They can brush their teeth independently and can manage bathroom needs on their own. They may begin to take on small household tasks, like making their bed or setting the table. They are confident in their abilities and may take on challenges with enthusiasm.
